Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I feel like I don't know myself anymore
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

issues.explanation: The Threat items describe a chronic interpersonal/home-intrusion danger template (monitoring for someone entering the home, planning escape routes, feeling unsafe specifically at night), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster. These items imply fear of human attack rather than disaster-related threat.

Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure could occur after a disaster, but in combination with the highly interpersonal Threat items it reinforces a different trauma narrative than natural disaster. The Memory items are disaster-compatible, but the Threat cluster is not clinically coherent with that trauma context.

The threat items are centered on anticipating intentional human intrusion or attack (planning escape routes, listening for someone entering the home), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster. Heightened alertness to loud sounds could fit disaster trauma, but these two more specific threat beliefs imply a different trauma context.

The appraisal 'The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down' is possible after a disaster, but in this profile it pulls toward a betrayal/response-failure formulation that is not supported elsewhere by the selected threat or memory items. Combined with the intrusion-focused threat items, it weakens coherence with a natural-disaster trauma profile.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: The threat item about listening for someone entering the home implies an interpersonal/intrusion danger theme that is hard to reconcile with a primary trauma type of natural disaster. For a natural-disaster profile, loud sounds and generalized hypervigilance are plausible, but specifically monitoring for a person entering the home suggests a different trauma context.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: The appraisal that institutions failed to protect him is possible after a disaster, but in combination with the home-intrusion threat cue it contributes to a mixed interpersonal-threat profile rather than a coherent natural-disaster formulation. The rest of the profile centers on terror, overwhelm, and disorganized memory, so this item is questionable mainly because it pulls toward a different trauma narrative when paired with the flagged threat item.

vignette:
Mark has been a military medic for twenty years, a man who defined himself by his ability to bring order to chaos. Now, six months after returning from a disaster relief deployment, the chaos was inside him. At forty-five, he felt like a stranger inhabiting his own life, the man he used to be lost somewhere in the rubble of a collapsed primary school. The earthquake had hit without warning, and his unit was among the first on the scene. He remembers the dust, thick and chalky, and the sounds—a dreadful grinding of concrete and rebar, punctuated by cries that were quickly swallowed by the unstable structure. He’d spent fourteen hours inside the ruins, crawling through spaces that were constantly shifting, the world a disorienting maze of broken desks and fallen ceiling tiles.

The memories don't arrive as a coherent story. Instead, they ambush him as sensory fragments, a jumble of images and sounds he cannot place in the right order. He’ll be cleaning his rifle and suddenly feel the phantom weight of a small, cold hand in his, or hear the high-pitched shriek of stressed metal that preceded the secondary collapse. When these flashes come, the same raw terror he felt in that darkness washes over him, so absolute and suffocating that he has to physically brace himself, shutting his eyes and forcing his mind onto something else, anything else, until the wave of emotion subsides. He has learned that trying to piece the events together is impossible; the sequence is lost to him, a confused reel of his worst moments playing on a loop.

This disjointed horror has become the lens through which he now views himself and the world. Each terrifying, chaotic memory fragment serves as fresh evidence for a verdict he has already passed: that he is a failure. The medic who was cool under fire, the man who could stabilize a patient in the back of a bouncing Humvee, was gone. In his place was someone who had failed to save a child pinned under a concrete beam. The memory of her face, of the moment the light left her eyes, confirms his belief that his skills are meaningless in a world so fundamentally cruel and random. His entire belief system—in duty, in competence, in the idea that good people could make a difference—has been completely destroyed. He no longer feels like a medic; he doesn’t know who he is anymore.

This profound sense of a broken identity and a meaningless world now dictates which parts of the past he can even access. His mind, convinced of his own failure, selectively retrieves only the evidence that supports this conclusion. He cannot recall the faces of the twelve people he did pull from the rubble, only the one he lost. This bleak outlook ensures that when the memory is triggered, it is always the most painful, chaotic, and incriminating fragments that surface, which in turn reinforces his conviction that he is irrevocably broken. The constant, low-level hum of being on guard also feeds this despair. Even in the relative quiet of the base, he cannot relax. Any unexpected sound—a dropped tray in the mess hall, a truck backfiring on the perimeter road—sends a jolt of adrenaline through him, his body tensing for an impact that never comes. This unending hypervigilance makes it impossible to feel safe, subtly confirming his new belief that the world is an inherently dangerous place and that he is no longer equipped to navigate it.

His life has shrunk as a result. He avoids his comrades, taking his meals back to his room, the easy camaraderie of the barracks now feeling like a language he no longer speaks. His commanding officer has put him on notice for performance issues, citing a lack of focus and engagement during training exercises. It was this formal warning that finally broke through his isolation. Mark came to therapy not with any real hope, but with the quiet fear that he was right, that the man he was is gone for good, and a desperate, unspoken plea to find out if there is anything left to salvage.
